reference.one_line: 36-year-old woman, 10 hours after a third vaginal birth complicated by 1,800 mL atonic haemorrhage; balloon in place, transfused, stable, awaiting staged deflation at 15:00.

handoff.summary: Ottilie Pellowe-Ansah, 36, gave birth at 04:20 today after induction and bled 1,800 mL from a uterus that would not contract. She had oxytocin, methylergometrine, one dose of carboprost (which set off her asthma: wheeze, saturation 91%), two doses of tranexamic acid, then a 400 mL uterine balloon under general anaesthesia at 05:55, with 3 red cells, 2 plasma and 1 cryoprecipitate pool. Now pulse 86, blood pressure 118/72, room air, uterus firm, drain nil since 11:00, urine over 100 mL/h, haemoglobin 8.9, fibrinogen 290. Two loose ends: the 12:00 enoxaparin 40 mg has not been given, and the as-needed carboprost order is still active. Baby girl is with her and breastfeeding.
to_do: Ask the resident about the uncharted 12:00 enoxaparin dose (timing relative to balloon removal)
Get the carboprost order discontinued and carboprost added to her intolerances
Resident at the bedside at 15:00 for staged deflation: remove 200 mL, watch 30 minutes, then balloon and pack out
Hourly observations, uterine tone, pad and drain; oxytocin 125 mL/h until 2 hours after removal, then catheter out
Acetaminophen due 15:00; blood count and clotting at 18:00; fasting glucose tomorrow
Help with every breastfeed; not to stand without 2 staff
if_then: If bleeding returns on deflation or the uterus softens, then re-inflate, massage, call the attending and anaesthetist: back to theatre, interventional radiology on notice; 2 red cell units are crossmatched
If the uterus is soft, then do not give carboprost and no anti-inflammatory painkillers
If pulse is over 120, systolic under 90 or wheeze returns, then call the anaesthetist; albuterol nebuliser as ordered
If urine is under 30 mL/h for 2 hours, then call the resident

reference.brief_hospital_course: Ms Pellowe-Ansah, 36, in her third pregnancy, was admitted on 16 Nov 2026 at 39 weeks 3 days for induction of labour for a large baby (estimated 4,150 g) with diet-controlled gestational diabetes. She has moderate persistent asthma and bled 700 mL after her 2022 birth. After membrane rupture and almost 16 hours of oxytocin she gave birth vaginally at 04:20 on 17 Nov to a girl of 4,280 g. The placenta was complete, but the uterus failed to contract and she lost a measured 1,800 mL. Treatment was massage, oxytocin infusion, methylergometrine, tranexamic acid twice and a single dose of carboprost, which had been listed as a drug to avoid and was followed within five minutes by wheeze and saturation 91%, treated with oxygen and albuterol. The major haemorrhage call was activated at 05:20, although the weighed loss had passed 1,000 mL by 05:00. Under general anaesthesia the cavity was found empty and a balloon was filled with 400 mL at 05:55, with prompt control. She received 3 units of red cells, 2 of plasma and 1 cryoprecipitate pool for a haemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL and fibrinogen 185 mg/dL; at 10:00 these were 8.9 and 290. A first-degree tear was sutured. At the time of writing she is stable on the high-dependency bay, breastfeeding, awaiting balloon removal; enoxaparin due at 12:00 has not yet been given.

problem_list.problem: Postpartum haemorrhage 1,800 mL from uterine atony; balloon tamponade in place
Acute blood-loss anaemia, haemoglobin 7.4 then 8.9 g/dL after 3 units
Asthma with bronchospasm after carboprost; order still active
Raised clot risk after birth; first enoxaparin dose overdue
Distress after a frightening birth and separation from baby

reconciled_medications.reason: Wheeze at 05:00 and 07:40; chest clear since.

reconciled_medications.reason: Until 2 hours after the balloon is removed, then stop.

reconciled_medications.reason: Caused bronchospasm in a woman with asthma; anaesthetist asked for the order to be reviewed.

reconciled_medications.medicine: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for 10 days
reconciled_medications.reason: Criteria met at 10:00 (platelets 142, fibrinogen 290, no bleeding); the 12:00 dose is overdue and must be given or its delay justified.
Only safe simple painkiller for her.
Aspirin-sensitive asthma; on hold as a do-not-give order.

reconciled_medications.medicine: Tranexamic acid, methylergometrine, cefazolin, calcium gluconate (single doses)

Blood count and coagulation with fibrinogen at 18:00
Debrief with Dr. Vasquez-Tolland and written summary before discharge; mood check before home and at 2 weeks

qa.q: What was the total measured blood loss?
qa.a: 1,800 mL, final at 06:30, measured by weighing pads and the drape.

qa.q: Which blood products did she receive?
qa.a: 3 units of red cells, 2 units of plasma and 1 pool of cryoprecipitate; two more red cell units remain crossmatched.
evidence: path: Blood bank major haemorrhage issue report

qa.q: How much is in the uterine balloon, and when was it placed?
qa.a: 400 mL of warmed saline, placed at 05:55 on 17 Nov with a vaginal pack.

qa.q: What is the baby's birth weight and condition at birth?
qa.a: A girl, 4,280 g, born 04:20, scores of 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes; glucose 52, 58 and 61 mg/dL at 2, 4 and 6 hours.

qa.q: How did her haemoglobin change across the admission?
qa.a: 11.8 g/dL on admission, 10.8 at 04:50, 7.4 at 06:15, 8.9 at 10:00 after three units.

qa.q: What happened to fibrinogen and lactate?
qa.a: Fibrinogen 310, then 185, then 290 mg/dL after plasma and cryoprecipitate. Lactate 2.8, 3.4, then 1.3 mmol/L.
10 to 20 mL per check between 05:15 and 06:00 during the bleed, recovering to 90 to 130 mL an hour from 09:00.

qa.q: In what order and at what times were the drugs to contract the uterus given?
qa.a: Oxytocin 10 units intramuscular 04:21; oxytocin infusion 04:35; methylergometrine 0.2 mg 04:42; carboprost 250 micrograms 04:55.

qa.q: How long after carboprost did she become wheezy?
qa.a: About five minutes: carboprost at 04:55, wheeze and saturation 91% at 05:00.

qa.q: How long from birth to balloon placement?
Does she meet the conditions set for starting enoxaparin?
qa.a: Yes. The conditions were no further bleeding, platelets above 75 and fibrinogen above 200; at 10:00 platelets were 142, fibrinogen 290 and loss was scant.

qa.q: Why is she on acetaminophen alone for pain?
qa.a: She has aspirin-sensitive asthma and wheezes with ibuprofen, so ibuprofen and ketorolac are do-not-give.
evidence: orders: Ibuprofen and ketorolac, do not give

qa.q: What were her glucose readings during labour?
qa.a: The chart does not record them. The plan was checks every 2 hours in labour, but only laboratory values (92, 128, 104 mg/dL) appear.

qa.q: Who gave the verbal order for carboprost?
qa.a: Not recorded. The dose is charted as 'verbal order' without a name; Dr. Ekwueme-Hart was present from 04:38, but the record does not say he ordered it.

tasks.prompt: Review the medicines used during the haemorrhage, and the orders still active, against her medical history.
expected_findings: Carboprost was given at 04:55 by verbal order although she has moderate persistent asthma and the admission plan (and 2022 and booking records) say to avoid it
Within five minutes she had wheeze and saturation 91%, needing 15 L oxygen and albuterol
The as-needed order (every 15 minutes, up to 8 doses) is still active although the anaesthetist asked for it to be reviewed
Carboprost is not on her allergy and intolerance list
acceptable_actions: Discontinue the carboprost order and record the reaction on the allergy list
Tell the resident and attending; make sure the deflation team knows the alternatives if she bleeds again
must_not: Leave the order active as a backup for deflation
Call the tranexamic acid doses the error

tasks.prompt: Check whether every scheduled medicine due so far today has been given.
expected_findings: Enoxaparin 40 mg, first dose due 12:00, is uncharted at 14:30 with no reason recorded
The conditions were met on the 10:00 bloods (platelets 142, fibrinogen 290, no further bleeding) and the 11:00 note says to give it
She is at raised clot risk: haemorrhage, transfusion, age over 35, bed rest
acceptable_actions: Ask the resident now whether to give it at once or time it around the 15:00 balloon removal, and document the decision
must_not: Cancel clot prevention because she bled this morning
Add heparin on top of the enoxaparin order

tasks.prompt: Check that the blood loss is recorded consistently across the notes and flowsheets.
expected_findings: The operative note gives a total blood loss of 1,200 mL
The flowsheet, intake and output, event record, progress note and nursing note all give a measured 1,800 mL
acceptable_actions: Ask Dr. Vasquez-Tolland to add a correction to the operative note
Use 1,800 mL in the debrief and discharge summary
must_not: Add the figures together to make 3,000 mL

tasks.prompt: Work out when the measured blood loss first exceeded 1,000 mL and compare it with the time the major haemorrhage call went out.
expected_findings: The weighed running total was 800 mL at 04:45 and 1,150 mL at 05:00, so 1,000 mL was passed between 04:45 and 05:00
The event record says the loss passed 1,000 mL at 05:20, when the call was activated (blood bank logged 05:21); the total was already 1,400 mL at 05:15
The call, and so the first red cells (running 05:28), came about 20 minutes late
acceptable_actions: State the corrected time and flag it for the case review
must_not: Accept 05:20 as the time the threshold was crossed
Blame the blood bank, which issued the first unit five minutes after the call

tasks.prompt: Look for duplicated doses among the medicines given during the haemorrhage.
expected_findings: Tranexamic acid 1 g was given at 05:02 and again at 05:40, 38 minutes apart
This is correct: the order allows one repeat after 30 minutes if bleeding continues, and both doses were within 3 hours of the 04:20 birth
acceptable_actions: No action; note that no third dose is due
must_not: Report the second dose as a duplicate or an overdose
evidence: meds: Tranexamic acid sig and doses

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: Dr. Ekwueme-Hart arrived at 15:05, read the medication record before touching the balloon and found both problems. He stopped the carboprost order, added the reaction to her allergy list and chose to delay enoxaparin until after removal. Deflation went smoothly: the balloon and pack were out by 15:45 with 60 mL of loss and a firm uterus. Evening bloods were stable and enoxaparin was given at 18:40. She walked the next morning, a little light-headed. The attending held a full debrief on 18 Nov and corrected the operative note to 1,800 mL. She went home on 19 Nov, breastfeeding, with iron and enoxaparin to 26 Nov. Heavier bleeding on 25 Nov brought her to the assessment unit, where a scan showed an empty uterus. At two weeks she described intrusive memories of the birth and was referred to perinatal mental health. No clot occurred.

events.event: Resident stops the carboprost order, records the reaction; enoxaparin deferred until after balloon removal
Balloon and pack removed after staged deflation; loss 60 mL, uterus firm
Oxytocin stopped, catheter out; haemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, platelets 151, fibrinogen 320 mg/dL
First enoxaparin 40 mg given, 6 hours 40 minutes late
Fasting glucose 88 mg/dL; walked with two staff
Debrief with Dr. Vasquez-Tolland and both parents; operative note corrected to 1,800 mL
Discharged home with baby (baby weight loss 6%)
Assessment unit visit for heavier bleeding with a clot: ultrasound shows no retained tissue, haemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, sent home
Two-week check: intrusive memories and poor sleep; referred to perinatal mental health

outcomes_30_day.notable: No clot or further transfusion; exclusively breastfeeding; birth-related trauma symptoms under perinatal mental health care.

portal_messages.subject: Induction on the 16th - a few worries
portal_messages.body: Hi, I saw the doctor yesterday about the baby being big and I'm booked for induction on Monday. Two things are going round my head. Do I keep using my asthma inhaler on the day? And last time I bled a lot and they said there was one injection I couldn't have because of my chest. Will whoever is on that night know that? I don't want to be explaining it mid-contraction. Thanks, Ottilie
ideal_reply_points: Keep taking the regular inhaler and bring both inhalers
Confirm the record says to avoid carboprost and anti-inflammatory painkillers, and that it will be on the induction plan
Explain the bleeding precautions: drip, blood sample held, injection after birth, haemorrhage kit in the room
Invite her to remind staff on arrival

portal_messages.subject: Re: Induction on the 16th - a few worries
portal_messages.body: Hello Ottilie, sensible questions. Yes, keep taking your regular inhaler morning and evening, including Monday, and bring it and your blue one with you. Your notes say clearly, from your booking visit, that the injection called carboprost should be avoided because of your asthma, and that you can't have ibuprofen. Because of last time you will have a drip in, a blood sample held ready and the usual injection as baby is born. Do still mention it when you arrive.
ideal_reply_points: Names the drug so she can recognise it
Encourages her to speak up on the day

portal_messages.subject: Bleeding heavier today
portal_messages.body: Sorry if this is nothing. The bleeding had gone brownish but since this morning it's bright red again and I just passed a clot about the size of a golf ball. I'm changing a pad every two hours or so. No temperature, not dizzy, tummy a bit crampy. I'm still on the blood thinner injections until tomorrow. After last week I'm scared to ignore it. Do I wait and see?
ideal_reply_points: Do not wait: come to the assessment unit today, with someone else driving
Go straight to emergency care or call an ambulance if soaking a pad an hour, more large clots, faint, or short of breath
Do not take tonight's enoxaparin until she has been seen

portal_messages.subject: Re: Bleeding heavier today
portal_messages.body: Ottilie, you were right to write. With your history and the injections we'd like to see you this afternoon, please don't wait. Come to the assessment unit and let Kwabena drive. Bring the baby, and bring your pads so we can see the loss. Hold today's injection until we've checked you. If you soak a pad in an hour, pass more big clots or feel faint or breathless, call an ambulance instead. I've told the unit to expect you.
ideal_reply_points: Same-day assessment with a named place

portal_messages.subject: Worried about Ottilie
portal_messages.body: This is Kwabena, Ottilie's husband, using her login with her agreement. She isn't sleeping even when the baby does. She keeps going over the birth, says she can still see the room filling up with people, and cries most evenings. She won't let the baby out of her sight. She says she is fine. She has never been like this. Is this normal after what happened and what should I do?
ideal_reply_points: Thank him; these reactions are common after a frightening birth and are treatable
Ask directly about thoughts of harming herself or the baby; if present, urgent help today
Phone contact within a day and bring the mood check forward
Offer support for him too, since he described the birth as the worst hour of his life

conversation.setting: Postnatal high-dependency bay, bed LP-02, early afternoon 17 Nov; baby asleep in the cot

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Hello, I'm the social worker for the unit. The midwives asked me to come by after this morning. Is this a bad moment? I can see she's just gone down.

turns.speaker: Ottilie
turns.text: No, stay. She's asleep at last. This is Kwabena.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Hello, Kwabena. I'm not here to go through the medical side. I'd just like to hear how it was for both of you. Ottilie, what do you remember?

turns.speaker: Ottilie
turns.text: The birth, all of it, that part was fine. Then she was on my chest and then the room just filled up with people. And I was so cold. And I couldn't get my breath, I kept saying I can't breathe.

turns.speaker: Kwabena
turns.text: They took the baby off her and gave her to me, and then they said I had to wait outside, they were taking Ottilie to theatre.

turns.speaker: Ottilie
turns.text: I didn't see her again until, what, half seven? That's the bit. Three hours. That's the bit I can't...

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Take your time.

turns.speaker: Ottilie
turns.text: Did I do something wrong? Should I have said something sooner, about the bleeding?

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: You've asked me that twice now, so I know it's sitting heavy. Nothing I've heard suggests you did anything wrong. But I want Dr. Vasquez-Tolland to answer that properly, with the facts in front of her.

turns.speaker: Kwabena
turns.text: I had her on my chest, skin to skin, the midwife showed me. An hour, more. Nobody could tell me anything. Honestly, worst hour of my life.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Have you slept at all?

turns.speaker: Kwabena
turns.text: No. Every time I shut my eyes.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: What you're both describing, going over it, feeling shaky, not sleeping, is very common after a frightening birth. It doesn't mean something is wrong with you. Mostly it eases; sometimes it hangs on, and then we help.

turns.speaker: Ottilie
turns.text: Can I ask you something? My asthma's been really good all year. Why did my chest go like that, right in the middle of it?

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: That's a fair question and I'm not the right person to answer it. The medical team will go through each medicine you were given at the debrief. I'll make sure it's on their list.

turns.speaker: Ottilie
turns.text: Please. I want it written down as well. I won't take it in otherwise.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: A written summary. I'll ask for that. Now, home. Who's got the older two?

turns.speaker: Ottilie
turns.text: My mum. They're seven and four. She can stay two weeks.

turns.speaker: Kwabena
turns.text: And I've got three weeks' leave.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Good. Any worries about money or the house while you're both off?

turns.speaker: Kwabena
turns.text: No, we're okay there.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: And Ottilie, before this, any low mood or anxiety, after the other two or any other time?

turns.speaker: Ottilie
turns.text: No. Never. I'm normally the calm one.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: All right. So, to check I've got it: the worst part for you was the gap before you saw her, and you both want the doctor to sit down and explain what happened, in writing too.

turns.speaker: Ottilie
turns.text: Yes. And the chest thing.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: And the chest thing. Someone will check how you're feeling before you go home and again at two weeks. I'll leave this leaflet about recovering after a difficult birth, and I'll come back tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Kwabena
turns.text: Thank you. Really.
